notes: Hand-curated by the TRAILS team. Facts are limited to well-established, widely documented history; every record links to its Wikipedia article. Coordinates are curated approximations of each site's centre and are checked against Wikipedia by scripts/verify_sources.py. 'significance' and 'kind' are curatorial judgements, not sourced facts. Imported places: records with origin='wikidata' were added automatically by scripts/merge_more_places.py from Wikidata (classes, inception, style, coordinates) and the Wikipedia lead (summary, history, CC BY-SA); their significance and kind come from Wikimedia sitelink counts, a popularity proxy, and they were not reviewed by hand.

places.name: Pantheon
places.summary: A Roman temple rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian, crowned by the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world and lit by a single open oculus.
places.then_now: Built as a temple to the gods of Rome, it was consecrated as a church in 609 AD, which is a major reason it survives almost intact.
places.history: The portico still carries the inscription naming Marcus Agrippa, who built an earlier temple on the site, but the present building dates from Hadrian's reign. In 609 the Byzantine emperor Phocas gave it to Pope Boniface IV, who turned it into the church of St Mary and the Martyrs. The painter Raphael is buried inside, as are the first two kings of unified Italy.

places.name: Piazza della Rotonda
places.summary: The square in front of the Pantheon, centred on a fountain by Giacomo della Porta topped with an ancient Egyptian obelisk.
places.then_now: Once a crowded market square hemmed in by shops, it is now one of the busiest gathering points in the historic centre.
places.history: Giacomo della Porta designed the fountain in the 1570s. In 1711, under Pope Clement XI, it was remodelled to carry an Egyptian obelisk of Ramesses II, one of the many ancient obelisks re-erected by the popes.

places.name: Colosseum
places.summary: The Flavian Amphitheatre, the largest amphitheatre ever built in the Roman world, used for gladiatorial games and public spectacles.
places.then_now: Where tens of thousands once watched games, the stripped-back arena floor now exposes the underground passages that held animals and stage machinery.
places.history: Construction began under Emperor Vespasian and the amphitheatre was inaugurated in 80 AD under his son Titus, with further work under Domitian. Earthquakes and centuries of stone robbing removed much of the outer ring; the travertine was reused in buildings across Rome.

places.name: Arch of Constantine
places.summary: A triumphal arch dedicated to Constantine the Great after his victory at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312.
places.then_now: It once marked the triumphal route into the city; today it stands beside the Colosseum on a pedestrian-friendly stretch.
places.history: Much of its sculpture was taken from earlier monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius and reused, a practice known as spolia. It is the largest surviving Roman triumphal arch.

places.name: Arch of Titus
places.summary: A single-bay arch on the Via Sacra commemorating Titus, whose relief panels show the spoils of the Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD.
places.then_now: Built over the Sacred Way into the Forum, it was later absorbed into medieval fortifications and restored as a free-standing arch in the 19th century.
places.history: Emperor Domitian built the arch shortly after the death of his brother Titus. The inner reliefs depicting the menorah carried in triumph are among the best-known images of Roman state art. Giuseppe Valadier restored it in the 1820s.

places.name: Roman Forum
places.summary: The rectangular plaza at the heart of ancient Rome, surrounded by the ruins of temples, basilicas and government buildings.
places.then_now: The centre of Roman public life became a cattle pasture known as the Campo Vaccino before excavations from the 18th century onward uncovered it again.
places.history: For centuries the Forum hosted elections, trials, speeches and triumphal processions. After the fall of the Western Empire its buildings decayed or were converted into churches, and the ground level rose by several metres until systematic excavation began.

places.name: Arch of Septimius Severus
places.summary: A triple arch at the north-west end of the Forum celebrating Septimius Severus and his sons' victories over the Parthians.
places.then_now: In the Middle Ages part of the arch belonged to a church and was half buried; today it stands fully exposed at the Forum's Capitoline end.
places.history: The dedicatory inscription originally named Septimius Severus and both his sons, Caracalla and Geta. After Caracalla had Geta murdered in 211, Geta's name was erased and replaced, an example of damnatio memoriae still traceable in the inscription.

places.name: Temple of Antoninus and Faustina
places.summary: A Roman temple in the Forum dedicated to Empress Faustina and later also to her husband Antoninus Pius, with a Baroque church façade rising behind its columns.
places.then_now: Converted into the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda, it shows two eras at once: an ancient colonnade fronting an early-17th-century façade.
places.history: Antoninus Pius dedicated the temple to his deified wife Faustina after her death in 140/141; after his own death the Senate rededicated it to both. Its conversion into a church is why the portico survived.

sources.title: Temple of Antoninus and Faustina — Wikipedia

places.name: Curia Julia
places.summary: The Senate house of ancient Rome, begun by Julius Caesar; the present brick building is Diocletian's reconstruction after a fire.
places.then_now: It survived because it was turned into the church of Sant'Adriano in the 7th century; 20th-century restoration removed the church additions.
places.history: Caesar began the building as part of his reorganisation of the Forum, and Augustus completed it. Its conversion into a church preserved the structure, while its bronze doors were moved in the 17th century to the Archbasilica of St John Lateran.

places.name: Mamertine Prison
places.summary: An ancient prison beneath the church of San Giuseppe dei Falegnami, where enemies of Rome such as Vercingetorix were held before execution.
places.then_now: The underground cell of the Tullianum is now visited through the church above, and Christian tradition associates it with the imprisonment of Saints Peter and Paul.
places.history: The lower chamber, the Tullianum, is one of the oldest structures in Rome. Ancient sources record that the Gallic leader Vercingetorix was held there before his execution after Caesar's triumph.

places.name: Temple of Venus and Roma
places.summary: Once the largest temple in ancient Rome, designed by Emperor Hadrian on the Velian Hill between the Forum and the Colosseum.
places.then_now: Its platform now offers a view straight onto the Colosseum; part of the site is occupied by the church of Santa Francesca Romana.
places.history: The temple had two back-to-back cellae, one for Venus Felix and one for Roma Aeterna. Ancient tradition holds that Hadrian disputed its design with the architect Apollodorus of Damascus.

sources.title: Temple of Venus and Roma — Wikipedia

places.name: Palatine Hill
places.built: Settled from the early first millennium BC; imperial palaces from the 1st century AD
places.summary: The centremost of Rome's seven hills, site of the earliest settlement and later of the emperors' palaces; the word 'palace' derives from its name.
places.then_now: Imperial residences once covered the hill; today it is an archaeological park of ruins, gardens and views over the Forum and the Circus Maximus.
places.history: According to legend Romulus founded the city here, and archaeology has found Iron Age huts on the hill. Augustus lived on the Palatine, and Domitian's vast palace complex dominated it from the late 1st century AD.

places.name: Circus Maximus
places.summary: Ancient Rome's largest chariot-racing stadium, laid out in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine hills.
places.then_now: The racetrack's outline survives as a long grassy park used for concerts and public celebrations.
places.history: The circus was rebuilt and enlarged many times, notably by Julius Caesar and Trajan. Two Egyptian obelisks once stood on its central barrier; both were moved in the 16th century and now stand in Piazza del Popolo and outside the Lateran.

places.name: Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine
places.summary: The largest building in the Roman Forum, whose three surviving coffered vaults show the scale of late Roman engineering.
places.then_now: Once a civic hall for courts and business, only the north aisle stands today and is used as a summer concert venue.
places.history: Emperor Maxentius began the basilica and Constantine completed it after defeating him in 312. A colossal statue of Constantine stood inside; fragments of it are displayed in the Capitoline Museums.

places.name: Trajan's Column
places.summary: A marble column whose spiral relief frieze narrates Emperor Trajan's wars against the Dacians.
places.then_now: Trajan's statue once crowned the column; since 1587 a statue of St Peter has stood at the top.
places.history: The column stood within Trajan's Forum, and its base served as the tomb for the emperor's ashes. The continuous frieze is a key visual source for the Roman army's equipment and campaigns.

places.name: Trajan's Market
places.summary: A multi-storey brick complex built into the slope of the Quirinal Hill alongside Trajan's Forum, often described as one of the world's oldest shopping centres.
places.then_now: Reused as housing and fortifications in the Middle Ages, it now houses the Museum of the Imperial Fora.
places.history: The complex is usually attributed to the architect Apollodorus of Damascus. Its exact original function is debated; it likely combined administrative offices with shops.

places.name: Via dei Fori Imperiali
places.summary: A broad avenue cut between Piazza Venezia and the Colosseum, running over and alongside the remains of the Imperial Fora.
places.then_now: Laid out under the Fascist regime by demolishing a dense medieval and Renaissance neighbourhood, it is now often closed to traffic and a natural walking axis.
places.history: The road was inaugurated in 1932 as the Via dell'Impero. Its construction destroyed historic housing and buried parts of the ancient fora, which later excavations have partly uncovered.

places.name: Vittoriano (Altare della Patria)
places.summary: A monumental white-marble complex honouring Victor Emmanuel II, the first king of unified Italy, and home to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
places.then_now: Its construction cleared part of the medieval Capitoline slope; today it holds museums and a terrace with panoramic views of Rome.
places.history: Giuseppe Sacconi won the design competition, and the monument was inaugurated in 1911 for the 50th anniversary of unification, though work continued until 1935. The Unknown Soldier was buried here in 1921.

places.name: Palazzo Venezia
places.summary: One of the first great Renaissance palaces in Rome, built for Cardinal Pietro Barbo, later Pope Paul II.
places.then_now: Once the Venetian embassy and later Mussolini's headquarters, whose balcony he used for speeches, it now houses the National Museum of Palazzo Venezia.
places.history: The palace takes its name from its long use as the seat of the Republic of Venice's ambassadors. Mussolini used it as his office, and the balcony over the piazza became associated with his public addresses.

places.name: Piazza del Campidoglio
places.summary: Michelangelo's square on the Capitoline Hill, flanked by the palaces of the Capitoline Museums and approached by the gentle ramp of the Cordonata.
places.then_now: The ancient religious heart of Rome became the seat of the city government, a role it still holds today.
places.history: Pope Paul III commissioned Michelangelo to redesign the hill, and the work was completed long after his death. The bronze equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius in the centre is a copy; the original is inside the Capitoline Museums.

places.name: Theatre of Marcellus
places.summary: An open-air theatre completed by Augustus and named after his nephew Marcellus, with Renaissance apartments built on top of its arcades.
places.then_now: Its curved ancient arcades still carry a 16th-century palace whose upper floors remain private residences.
places.history: Julius Caesar planned the theatre, and Augustus dedicated it to Marcellus, who had died young in 23 BC. In the Middle Ages it was used as a fortress, and Baldassare Peruzzi designed the palace built into it in the 16th century.

places.name: Portico of Octavia
places.summary: The surviving entrance of an ancient colonnaded walkway that Augustus dedicated to his sister Octavia, now at the heart of the Jewish Ghetto.
places.then_now: Its ruined propylaeum frames the church of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, named after the fish market that operated here for centuries.
places.history: The portico enclosed temples of Juno and Jupiter. From the Middle Ages the area hosted Rome's fish market, and from 1555 it lay at the edge of the Roman Ghetto established by Pope Paul IV.

places.name: Turtle Fountain
places.summary: A small late-Renaissance fountain in Piazza Mattei with four bronze youths lifting turtles into the upper basin.
places.then_now: Tucked into a quiet square in the old Ghetto area, it is easy to miss; the bronze turtles today are copies after thefts.
places.history: Giacomo della Porta designed the fountain and Taddeo Landini cast the bronze figures. The turtles were added in the 17th century and are traditionally attributed to Bernini or his circle.

places.name: Largo di Torre Argentina
places.summary: A sunken square holding four Republican-era temples and part of the Curia of Pompey, where Julius Caesar was assassinated in 44 BC.
places.then_now: Uncovered during demolitions in the 1920s, the ruins are now also home to a well-known cat sanctuary.
places.history: The temples, labelled A to D by archaeologists, are among the oldest in Rome. Behind temple B are the remains of the Curia of Pompey, the meeting hall where Caesar was killed on the Ides of March.

places.name: Church of the Gesù
places.summary: The mother church of the Jesuit order, whose design became a model for Baroque churches across Europe and the Americas.
places.then_now: Its restrained façade hides one of Rome's most theatrical ceilings, Baciccio's Triumph of the Name of Jesus.
places.history: Vignola designed the church and Giacomo della Porta the façade. The ceiling fresco by Giovanni Battista Gaulli (Baciccio) dates from the 1670s, and the church holds the tomb of Ignatius of Loyola, the order's founder.

places.name: Santa Maria sopra Minerva
places.summary: Rome's only major Gothic church, with a blue star-studded vault, Filippino Lippi's frescoes and Michelangelo's statue of the Risen Christ.
places.then_now: Its plain façade conceals a richly decorated Gothic interior; the church takes its name from a belief that it stood above a temple of Minerva.
places.history: The Dominican church contains the tomb of Saint Catherine of Siena and of the painter Fra Angelico. The Carafa Chapel was frescoed by Filippino Lippi in the late 15th century.

places.name: Elephant and Obelisk (Pulcino della Minerva)
places.summary: A marble elephant designed by Bernini carrying a small Egyptian obelisk, in the square in front of Santa Maria sopra Minerva.
places.then_now: The ancient obelisk was found in the grounds of the Dominican convent nearby and given a whimsical Baroque base; Romans nicknamed it the 'chick'.
places.history: Pope Alexander VII commissioned the monument; Bernini designed it and Ercole Ferrata carved it. The inscription on the base presents the elephant as a symbol that strength of mind is needed to support wisdom.

places.name: Temple of Hadrian
places.summary: Eleven Corinthian columns of a temple dedicated to the deified Hadrian, built into a later building on Piazza di Pietra.
places.then_now: The ancient colonnade forms the façade of a building that once housed papal customs offices and is now the Rome Chamber of Commerce.
places.history: Hadrian's adopted successor Antoninus Pius dedicated the temple. In the 17th century Carlo Fontana incorporated the surviving columns into the customs house of the Papal States.

places.name: Column of Marcus Aurelius
places.summary: A spiral-relief column in Piazza Colonna commemorating Marcus Aurelius's campaigns against Germanic tribes along the Danube.
places.then_now: It stands outside Palazzo Chigi, today the seat of the Italian Prime Minister; a statue of St Paul has topped it since 1589.
places.history: Modelled on Trajan's Column, its deeper-cut reliefs reflect late 2nd-century style. Pope Sixtus V had it restored and crowned with the statue of St Paul.

places.name: Trevi Fountain
places.summary: Rome's largest Baroque fountain, designed by Nicola Salvi, marking the end of the ancient Aqua Virgo aqueduct.
places.then_now: The aqueduct that feeds it was built in 19 BC by Agrippa; today millions of visitors throw coins into its basin, which are collected for charity.
places.history: Pope Clement XII held a competition in 1730 that Nicola Salvi won; the fountain was finished by Giuseppe Pannini in 1762. The central figure of Oceanus is by Pietro Bracci.

places.name: Spanish Steps
places.summary: A monumental stairway of 135 steps linking Piazza di Spagna with the church of Trinità dei Monti above.
places.then_now: Financed with a bequest from a French diplomat and named after the nearby Spanish embassy, the steps are now a protected monument where sitting is prohibited.
places.history: Francesco de Sanctis designed the steps, which were built in the 1720s with funds left by the French diplomat Étienne Gueffier. The square below takes its name from the Spanish Embassy to the Holy See.

places.name: Fontana della Barcaccia
places.summary: A half-sunken marble boat at the foot of the Spanish Steps, by Pietro Bernini, probably with his son Gian Lorenzo.
places.then_now: Because the aqueduct's water pressure here is low, the fountain was designed to sit below street level.
places.history: Pope Urban VIII commissioned the fountain, and the Barberini bees from his coat of arms appear on it. Tradition links its design to a boat left stranded here by a Tiber flood.

places.name: Trinità dei Monti
places.summary: A Renaissance church with twin bell towers at the top of the Spanish Steps, founded by the French king Louis XII.
places.then_now: Still a French institution, it is one of Rome's most photographed backdrops; the Sallustiano obelisk stands before it.
places.history: The church was built for the Minim friars under French royal patronage and has been under French administration since. The obelisk outside is a Roman-era imitation of Egyptian work, erected here in 1789.

places.name: Keats–Shelley House
places.summary: The house beside the Spanish Steps where the English poet John Keats died in 1821, now a museum of English Romantic poets.
places.then_now: The rooms Keats rented while seeking a cure for tuberculosis are now a small museum and library.
places.history: Keats arrived in Rome in late 1820 with the painter Joseph Severn and died here in February 1821, aged 25. The museum opened in 1909.

places.name: Piazza Navona
places.built: Follows the Stadium of Domitian (c. 86 AD); Baroque square 17th century
places.summary: A long oval square that preserves the shape of the ancient Stadium of Domitian, framed by Baroque fountains and churches.
places.then_now: Where athletes once competed, the square now hosts cafés, artists and a Christmas market; the stadium's remains lie beneath the buildings.
places.history: The square's outline follows Domitian's stadium of the 1st century AD. In the 17th century Pope Innocent X, whose family palace overlooked it, transformed it into a Baroque showpiece with Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers.

places.name: Fountain of the Four Rivers
places.summary: Bernini's fountain at the centre of Piazza Navona, with river gods representing the Nile, Ganges, Danube and Río de la Plata beneath an obelisk.
places.then_now: Commissioned to glorify Pope Innocent X, it remains the centrepiece of Rome's best-known Baroque square.
places.history: Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the fountain for Pope Innocent X; the figures were carved by his assistants. The popular story that a river god shields his eyes from Borromini's church opposite is a legend: the fountain was finished before the church façade was begun.

places.name: Sant'Agnese in Agone
places.summary: A Baroque church on Piazza Navona whose concave façade and dome are largely the work of Francesco Borromini.
places.then_now: Built as the Pamphilj family's church beside their palace, it still dominates the west side of the square.
places.history: Pope Innocent X commissioned the church; Carlo and Girolamo Rainaldi started it, and Borromini took over in 1653, redesigning the façade. It is dedicated to Saint Agnes, martyred according to tradition at this site.

places.name: Fontana del Moro
places.summary: The fountain at the south end of Piazza Navona, with a central figure wrestling a dolphin added to Giacomo della Porta's basin.
places.then_now: Its 16th-century basin later received a Baroque centrepiece; several original sculptures have been replaced with copies.
places.history: Giacomo della Porta built the basin in the 1570s. The central figure, known as the Moor, was designed by Bernini and carved by Giovanni Antonio Mari in the 1650s.

places.name: Fountain of Neptune (Piazza Navona)
places.summary: The fountain at the north end of Piazza Navona; its 16th-century basin stood without sculpture until Neptune and his companions were added in 1878.
places.then_now: For three centuries it was a plain basin; the 19th-century sculptures were added to balance the square's other two fountains.
places.history: Giacomo della Porta designed the basin in 1574. Antonio Della Bitta carved Neptune fighting an octopus and Gregorio Zappalà the surrounding figures in 1878.

places.name: Pasquino
places.summary: A battered ancient statue that became Rome's first 'talking statue', where anonymous satirical verses against the popes were posted.
places.then_now: Since the 16th century Romans have pinned anonymous satire to it; the word 'pasquinade' comes from its name, and notes still appear today.
places.history: The fragment was unearthed nearby and set up in 1501 by Cardinal Oliviero Carafa. Satirical poems attached to it gave rise to the term pasquinade.

places.name: Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza
places.summary: Borromini's masterpiece, with a star-shaped plan and a spiralling lantern, hidden in the courtyard of Rome's old university palace.
places.then_now: Built as the chapel of the Sapienza university, it now stands inside the Palazzo della Sapienza, which houses the State Archives.
places.history: Francesco Borromini designed the church for the university. Its interior geometry, based on interlocking triangles, and its corkscrew lantern made it one of the most original buildings of the Roman Baroque.

places.name: San Luigi dei Francesi
places.summary: The French national church in Rome, home to Caravaggio's three paintings of the life of St Matthew in the Contarelli Chapel.
places.then_now: Visitors come today mainly for the Caravaggio canvases, which still hang in the chapel they were painted for.
places.history: Caravaggio painted the Calling of St Matthew and the Martyrdom of St Matthew around 1599–1600, followed by The Inspiration of St Matthew. They were his first major public commission.

places.name: Sant'Agostino
places.summary: One of the first Renaissance churches in Rome, holding Caravaggio's Madonna of Loreto and Raphael's fresco of the prophet Isaiah.
places.then_now: An early Renaissance façade gives little hint of the masterpieces inside.
places.history: The church was rebuilt in the late 15th century for the Augustinians. Caravaggio's Madonna of Loreto (c. 1604–1606) caused controversy for showing pilgrims with dirty feet.

places.name: Santa Maria della Pace
places.summary: A small church near Piazza Navona with Raphael's Sibyls fresco, a Baroque façade by Pietro da Cortona and a cloister by Bramante.
places.then_now: Its curved Baroque porch pushes into a tiny piazza designed as a stage set; the adjoining cloister is used for exhibitions.
places.history: Pope Sixtus IV rebuilt the church in the 1480s. Bramante designed its cloister around 1500, and Pietro da Cortona added the façade and square for Pope Alexander VII.

places.name: Campo de' Fiori
places.summary: A lively market square where the philosopher Giordano Bruno was burned for heresy in 1600, commemorated by a hooded bronze statue.
places.then_now: Once a place of public executions, it now hosts a daily morning market and evening crowds.
places.history: Giordano Bruno was executed here by the Roman Inquisition in 1600. Ettore Ferrari's statue of him was erected in 1889, a symbol of freedom of thought in the new Italian state.

places.name: Palazzo Farnese
places.summary: One of the most important High Renaissance palaces in Rome, built for the Farnese family with contributions by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger and Michelangelo.
places.then_now: The family palace of Pope Paul III is now the French Embassy in Italy.
places.history: Antonio da Sangallo the Younger began the palace for Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, the future Paul III. Michelangelo designed the upper storey and cornice, and Annibale Carracci painted the celebrated gallery ceiling.

places.name: Sant'Andrea della Valle
places.summary: A major Baroque church whose dome is among the tallest in Rome, and the setting of the first act of Puccini's opera Tosca.
places.then_now: Opera lovers know it as the church of Tosca's opening scene; it remains an active basilica.
places.history: Carlo Maderno designed the dome, completed in the 1620s. Giovanni Lanfranco and Domenichino painted the dome and apse frescoes.

places.name: Tiber Island
places.summary: The only island in Rome's stretch of the Tiber, associated with healing since a temple of Asclepius was founded here in 291 BC.
places.then_now: The healing tradition continues: a hospital, the Fatebenefratelli, still occupies much of the island.
places.history: The Romans built a temple to the healing god Asclepius after a plague. The church of San Bartolomeo all'Isola later rose on the site of the temple, and the island is linked to both banks by ancient bridges.

places.name: Ponte Fabricio
places.summary: The oldest Roman bridge in Rome still in its original state, linking the Tiber Island to the left bank.
places.then_now: Still used by pedestrians more than two thousand years after it was built.
places.history: Lucius Fabricius, curator of roads, built it in 62 BC, as recorded in the inscription still on the bridge.

places.name: Temple of Portunus
places.summary: One of the best-preserved Roman temples, dedicated to Portunus, god of harbours, beside the ancient river port.
places.then_now: It survived because it became a church in the Middle Ages; it now stands in a small park by the Tiber.
places.history: The temple stood in the Forum Boarium, ancient Rome's cattle market and river port. It was converted into the church of Santa Maria Egiziaca in the 9th century.

places.name: Temple of Hercules Victor
places.summary: A round temple in the Forum Boarium and the oldest surviving marble building in Rome.
places.then_now: Long mistaken for a temple of Vesta because of its circular plan, it was used as a church in the Middle Ages.
places.history: The temple is built largely of Greek marble and is thought to have been dedicated to Hercules Victor. It became the church of Santo Stefano delle Carrozze and later Santa Maria del Sole.

places.name: Santa Maria in Cosmedin and the Mouth of Truth
places.summary: A medieval church with a Romanesque bell tower whose portico holds the Bocca della Verità, an ancient marble mask said to bite the hands of liars.
places.then_now: The marble disc, probably once an ancient drain cover, became a tourist ritual famous from the film Roman Holiday (1953).
places.history: The church served Rome's Greek community in the early Middle Ages, giving rise to the name Cosmedin. The Mouth of Truth was placed in the portico in the 17th century.

places.name: Arch of Janus
places.summary: A rare four-sided Roman arch that once sheltered a crossroads in the Forum Boarium.
places.then_now: Fortified by the Frangipani family in the Middle Ages, it now stands alone in a quiet corner near the river.
places.history: The arch is usually dated to the reign of Constantine or his successors. Its niches once held statues, and medieval additions on top were removed during 19th-century restoration.

places.name: Aventine Keyhole
places.summary: A keyhole in the gate of the Knights of Malta's Priory on the Aventine that perfectly frames the dome of St Peter's Basilica.
places.then_now: The square and priory church are the only completed architectural work of the engraver Giovanni Battista Piranesi.
places.history: Piranesi redesigned the Piazza dei Cavalieri di Malta and the priory church in the 1760s. Looking through the gate's keyhole shows a garden avenue leading the eye to St Peter's dome.

sources.title: Villa del Priorato di Malta — Wikipedia

places.name: Giardino degli Aranci
places.summary: A small orange-tree park on the Aventine Hill with one of the classic panoramic views across Rome.
places.then_now: Laid out within the walls of a medieval Savelli family fortress, it is now a quiet public garden.
places.history: The park was created in 1932 within the area of the fortress of the Savelli family, next to the early Christian basilica of Santa Sabina.

places.name: Pyramid of Cestius
places.summary: An Egyptian-style pyramid built as the tomb of the Roman magistrate Gaius Cestius, later incorporated into the Aurelian Walls.
places.then_now: It survived because it was built into the 3rd-century city walls; the Protestant Cemetery, where Keats is buried, lies beside it.
places.history: The pyramid reflects the Roman fashion for Egyptian forms after the conquest of Egypt in 30 BC. Its inscriptions record that it was built in 330 days.

places.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
places.summary: Built as the Mausoleum of Hadrian, the cylindrical building became a papal fortress, residence and prison.
places.then_now: Once linked to the Vatican by the fortified Passetto di Borgo corridor, it is now a national museum.
places.history: Hadrian built the mausoleum for himself and his family. It was later fortified, and popes used it as a refuge, including Clement VII during the Sack of Rome in 1527. Its name comes from a legendary vision of the Archangel Michael during a plague in 590.

places.name: Ponte Sant'Angelo
places.summary: Hadrian's bridge to his mausoleum, lined since the 17th century with ten Baroque angels carrying instruments of the Passion.
places.then_now: Once the main pilgrim route to St Peter's, it is now a pedestrian bridge.
places.history: Emperor Hadrian completed the bridge in 134 AD. Pope Clement IX commissioned Bernini to design the angel statues, carved by his workshop.

places.name: St. Peter's Basilica
places.summary: The Renaissance basilica in Vatican City built over the traditional burial site of Saint Peter, crowned by Michelangelo's dome.
places.then_now: It replaced a 4th-century basilica built under Constantine; today it is one of the largest churches in the world.
places.history: Bramante, Michelangelo, Carlo Maderno and Bernini were among its architects. Michelangelo designed the dome, completed after his death by Giacomo della Porta. The basilica holds Michelangelo's Pietà and Bernini's baldachin.

places.name: St. Peter's Square
places.summary: Bernini's vast square before St Peter's, embraced by curved colonnades and centred on an ancient Egyptian obelisk.
places.then_now: Designed to receive crowds for papal blessings, it still does so on major feast days.
places.history: Pope Alexander VII commissioned Bernini to design the square. The obelisk was brought to Rome under Caligula and moved here in 1586 under Pope Sixtus V.

places.name: Tempietto of San Pietro in Montorio
places.summary: Bramante's small circular shrine on the Janiculum, a defining building of the High Renaissance.
places.then_now: Marking the place traditionally linked to Saint Peter's martyrdom, it stands in a cloister courtyard now within the Spanish Academy.
places.history: Donato Bramante built the Tempietto around 1502 under the patronage of the Spanish monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella. Its classical proportions influenced later domed architecture.

places.name: Santa Maria in Trastevere
places.summary: One of Rome's oldest churches, famous for its 12th-century gold mosaics on the façade and in the apse.
places.then_now: At the heart of Trastevere's busiest square, it still serves as a parish church.
places.history: Tradition places one of the first churches in Rome on this site. The present building was rebuilt under Pope Innocent II in the 12th century, reusing ancient columns. Pietro Cavallini's mosaics of the life of the Virgin date from the late 13th century.

places.name: Piazza del Popolo
places.summary: A great oval square at Rome's former northern gate, centred on the Flaminio obelisk and framed by twin churches.
places.then_now: For centuries travellers arriving from the north entered Rome here; the square was also a place of public executions until the 19th century.
places.history: The obelisk of Ramesses II was brought to Rome by Augustus and moved here from the Circus Maximus in 1589. Giuseppe Valadier gave the square its neoclassical shape in the early 19th century.

places.name: Santa Maria del Popolo
places.summary: A Renaissance church beside the Porta del Popolo holding Caravaggio's Conversion of Saint Paul and Crucifixion of Saint Peter.
places.then_now: Its modest façade hides works by Raphael, Bernini, Pinturicchio and Caravaggio.
places.history: Pope Sixtus IV rebuilt the church in the 1470s. Raphael designed the Chigi Chapel, later completed by Bernini, and the Cerasi Chapel holds Caravaggio's two paintings of 1600–1601.

places.name: Ara Pacis Augustae
places.summary: The Altar of Augustan Peace, an altar decorated with reliefs of the imperial family and allegories of peace and plenty.
places.then_now: Reassembled from excavated fragments in the 1930s, it is now enclosed in a modern museum designed by Richard Meier.
places.history: The Senate commissioned the altar in 13 BC to honour Augustus's return from Hispania and Gaul, and it was consecrated in 9 BC. Fragments were recovered over centuries and reassembled under the Fascist regime in 1938.

places.name: Mausoleum of Augustus
places.summary: The circular tomb Augustus built for himself and his family on the Campus Martius.
places.then_now: Over the centuries it served as a fortress, garden and concert hall; it reopened to visitors after a long restoration.
places.history: Augustus began the mausoleum early in his rule, and his ashes were placed there after his death in 14 AD. It was later used by the Colonna family as a fortress and in the early 20th century as a concert hall.

places.name: Domus Aurea
places.summary: Emperor Nero's vast 'Golden House', built after the Great Fire of 64 AD and later buried beneath the Baths of Trajan.
places.then_now: Its painted rooms, rediscovered underground in the Renaissance, inspired the 'grotesque' style of decoration; today it is visited on guided tours.
places.history: After Nero's death his successors returned the land to public use; the Colosseum was built on the site of his artificial lake. Renaissance artists, including Raphael, lowered themselves into the buried rooms to study the frescoes.

places.name: San Pietro in Vincoli
places.summary: A basilica housing the chains said to have bound Saint Peter and Michelangelo's statue of Moses for the tomb of Pope Julius II.
places.then_now: A short walk from the Colosseum, it remains a place of pilgrimage and of art history in equal measure.
places.history: The church was consecrated in the 5th century to house the relic of the chains. Michelangelo's Moses (c. 1513–1515) was intended for a far larger tomb for Julius II that was never completed as planned.

places.name: Basilica of San Clemente
places.built: 12th-century church over a 4th-century basilica and Roman buildings
places.summary: A layered site: a 12th-century basilica built over a 4th-century church, itself above Roman buildings and a Mithraic temple.
places.then_now: Visitors descend through roughly two thousand years of history, from the medieval apse mosaic down to the Roman levels.
places.history: Irish Dominicans, who have run the church since the 17th century, began excavating the lower levels in 1857. The Mithraeum was used for the cult of Mithras in the 2nd and 3rd centuries.

places.name: Santa Maria Maggiore
places.summary: One of Rome's four major papal basilicas, preserving 5th-century mosaics within a later Baroque exterior.
places.then_now: An early Christian basilica in plan, it now presents an 18th-century façade by Ferdinando Fuga.
places.history: Pope Sixtus III built the basilica in the 430s; the mosaics of the nave and triumphal arch date from that time. Its campanile is the tallest in Rome.

places.name: Santa Maria della Vittoria
places.summary: A small Baroque church holding Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa in the Cornaro Chapel.
places.then_now: Bernini designed the chapel like a theatre, with members of the Cornaro family carved as spectators in side boxes.
places.history: Carlo Maderno designed the church. Bernini created the Cornaro Chapel between 1647 and 1652 for Cardinal Federico Cornaro.

places.name: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane
places.summary: Borromini's first independent commission, a tiny church famous for its undulating façade and oval coffered dome.
places.then_now: It sits at a busy crossroads marked by four late-16th-century corner fountains.
places.history: Borromini designed the church for the Spanish Trinitarian order; the façade was completed after his death in 1667.

sources.title: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane — Wikipedia

places.name: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
places.summary: A small oval church by Bernini, who is said to have regarded it as his most perfect work.
places.then_now: Built for the Jesuit novitiate, it faces the gardens of the Quirinal Palace.
places.history: Bernini designed the church for Cardinal Camillo Pamphilj. Its oval plan is set across the short axis, so the altar faces the entrance at close range.

places.name: Quirinal Palace
places.summary: A papal summer palace that became the royal palace of Italy and, since 1946, the official residence of the President of the Italian Republic.
places.then_now: Home in turn to popes, kings and presidents, it overlooks a square with ancient statues of the Dioscuri and an obelisk.
places.history: Pope Gregory XIII began the palace in 1583. After the capture of Rome in 1870 it became the residence of the Kings of Italy, and after the 1946 referendum that of the President.

places.name: Sistine Chapel
places.summary: The Sistine Chapel is a chapel in the Apostolic Palace, the pope's official residence in Vatican City. Originally known as the Cappella Magna, it takes its name from Pope Sixtus IV, who had it built between 1473 and 1481. Since that time, it has served as a place of both religious and functionary papal activity.
places.history: Today, it is the site of the papal conclave, the process by which a new pope is selected. The chapel's fame lies mainly in the frescoes that decorate its interior, most particularly the Sistine Chapel ceiling and The Last Judgment, both by

places.name: Vatican Museums
places.summary: The Vatican Museums are the public museums of the Vatican City. They display works from the immense collection amassed by the Catholic Church and the papacy throughout the centuries, including several of the best-known Roman sculptures and most important masterpieces of Renaissance art in the world.
places.history: The museums contain roughly 70,000 works, of which 20,000 are on display, and currently employ 640 people who work in 40 different administrative, scholarly, and restoration

places.name: Apostolic Palace
places.summary: The Apostolic Palace is the official residence of the Pope, the head of the Catholic Church, located in Vatican City. It is also known as the Papal Palace, the Palace of the Vatican and the Vatican Palace.
places.history: The Vatican itself refers to the building as the Palace of Sixtus V, in honor of Pope Sixtus V, who built most of the present form of the

places.name: Aurelian Walls
places.summary: The Aurelian Walls are a line of city walls built between AD 271 and AD 275 in Rome, Italy, during the reign of the Roman Emperor Aurelian. They superseded the earlier Servian Wall built during the 4th century BC.

places.name: Laocoön and His Sons
places.summary: The statue of Laocoön and His Sons, also called the Laocoön Group, has been one of the most famous ancient sculptures since it was excavated in Rome in 1506 and put on public display in the Vatican Museums, where it remains today.
places.history: The statue is very likely the same one praised in the highest terms by Pliny the Elder, the main Roman writer on art, who attributed it to Greek sculptors but did not say when it was created. The figures are nearly life-sized, with the entire group measuring just over 2 m in height. The sculpture depicts the Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons Antiphantes and Thymbraeus being attacked by sea

places.name: Trajan's Forum
places.summary: Trajan's Forum was the last of the Imperial fora to be constructed in ancient Rome. The architect Apollodorus of Damascus oversaw its construction.

places.name: Capitoline Wolf
places.summary: The Capitoline Wolf is a bronze sculpture depicting a scene from the legend of the founding of Rome. The sculpture shows a she-wolf suckling the mythical twin founders of Rome, Romulus and Remus.
places.history: According to the legend, when King Numitor, grandfather of the twins, was overthrown by his brother Amulius in Alba Longa, the usurper ordered them to be cast into the Tiber River. They were rescued by a she-wolf that cared for them until a herdsman, Faustulus, found and raised

places.name: Temple of Vesta
places.summary: The Temple of Vesta, or the aedes, was an ancient edifice in Rome, Italy. It is located in the Roman Forum near the Regia and the House of the Vestal Virgins. The Temple of Vesta housed Vesta's holy fire, which was a symbol of Rome's safety and prosperity. The temple has a circular footprint, making it a tholos.

places.name: Piazza Venezia
places.summary: Piazza Venezia is a central hub of Rome, Italy, in which several thoroughfares intersect, including the Via dei Fori Imperiali and the Via del Corso. It takes its name from the Palazzo Venezia, built by the Venetian Cardinal, Pietro Barbo alongside the church of Saint Mark, the patron saint of Venice.
places.history: The Palazzo Venezia served as the embassy of the Republic of Venice in

places.name: Servian Wall
places.summary: The Servian Wall is an ancient Roman defensive barrier constructed around the city of Rome in the early 4th century BC.
places.history: The wall was built of volcanic tuff and was up to 10 m (33 ft) in height in places, 3.6 m (12 ft) wide at its base, 11 km (6.8 mi) long, and is believed to have had 16 main gates, of which only one or two have survived, and enclosed a total area of 246 hectares. In the 3rd century AD it was superseded by the construction of the larger Aurelian Walls as the city of Rome grew beyond the boundary of the Servian

places.name: Cloaca Maxima
places.summary: The Cloaca Maxima or, less often, Maxima Cloaca, is one of the world's earliest sewage systems. Its name is related to that of Cloacina, a Roman goddess. Built during either the Roman Kingdom or early Roman Republic, it was constructed in Ancient Rome in order to drain local marshes and remove waste from the city.
places.history: It carried effluent to the River Tiber, which ran beside the city. The sewer started at the Forum Augustum and ended at the Ponte Rotto and Ponte Palatino. It began as an open air canal, but it developed into a much larger sewer over the course of time. Agrippa renovated and reconstructed much of the sewer. This would not be the only development in the sewers, by the first century AD all eleven Roman aqueducts were connected to the sewer. After the Roman Empire fell the sewer was still used. By the 19th century, it had become a tourist attraction. Some parts of the sewer are still used today. During its heyday, it was highly valued as a sacred symbol of Roman culture and Roman

places.name: Imperial fora
places.summary: The Imperial Fora are a series of monumental fora, constructed in Rome over a period of one and a half centuries, between 46 BC and 113 AD. The fora were the center of the Roman Republic and of the Roman Empire.

places.name: Santa Maria in Ara Coeli
places.summary: The Basilica of Saint Mary of the Altar in Heaven is a titular basilica and conventual church of the Franciscan Convent of Aracoeli located on the highest summit of the Capitoline Hill in Rome, Italy.

sources.title: Santa Maria in Ara Coeli — Wikipedia

places.history: From 1250 to 1798 it was the headquarters of the General Curia of the Order of Friars Minor as well as being one of the city's principal civic churches. It is still the designated church of the city council of Rome, which uses the ancient title of Senatus Populusque Romanus. The present cardinal priest of the Titulus Sanctæ Mariæ de Aracœli is Salvatore De

places.name: Via Sacra
places.summary: The Via Sacra was the main street of ancient Rome, leading from the top of the Capitoline Hill, through some of the most important religious sites of the Forum, to the Colosseum.

places.name: Domus Sanctae Marthae
places.summary: The Domus Sanctae Marthae is a building adjacent to St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City. Completed in 1996, during the pontificate of Pope John Paul II, it is named after Martha of Bethany, who was a sibling to Mary and Lazarus of Bethany.
places.history: The building functions as a guest house for clergy having business with the Holy See and as the temporary residence of members of the College of Cardinals while participating in a papal conclave to elect a new

places.name: Temple of Saturn
places.summary: The Temple of Saturn was an ancient Roman temple to the god Saturn, in what is now Rome, Italy. Its ruins stand at the foot of the Capitoline Hill at the western end of the Roman Forum. The original dedication of the temple is traditionally dated to 497 BC, but ancient writers disagreed greatly about the history of this site.

places.name: Villa Medici
places.summary: The Villa Medici is a sixteenth-century Italian Mannerist villa and an architectural complex with 7-hectare Italian garden, contiguous with the more extensive Borghese gardens, on the Pincian Hill next to Trinità dei Monti in the historic centre of Rome, Italy.

places.name: Villa Farnesina
places.summary: The Villa Farnesina is a Renaissance suburban villa in the Via della Lungara, in the district of Trastevere in Rome, central Italy. Built between 1506 and 1510 for Agostino Chigi, the Pope's wealthy Sienese banker, it was a novel type of suburban villa, subsidiary to his main Palazzo Chigi in the city.
places.history: It is especially famous for the rich frescos by Raphael and other High Renaissance artists that remain in

places.name: Santa Sabina
places.summary: The Basilica of Saint Sabina is a historic church on the Aventine Hill in Rome, Italy. It is a titular minor basilica and mother church of the Roman Catholic Order of Preachers, better known as the Dominicans.

places.name: Villa Borghese gardens
places.summary: Villa Borghese is a landscape garden in Rome, containing a number of buildings, museums and attractions. It is the third-largest public park in Rome, after the ones of the Villa Doria Pamphili and Villa Ada.
places.history: The gardens were developed for the Villa Borghese Pinciana, built by the architect Flaminio Ponzio, developing sketches by Scipione Borghese, who used it as a villa suburbana, or party villa, at the edge of Rome, and to house his art collection. The gardens as they are now were remade in the late 19th

places.name: Temple of Castor and Pollux
places.summary: The Temple of Castor and Pollux was an ancient temple in the Roman Forum, Rome, Central Italy. It was originally built in gratitude for victory at the Battle of Lake Regillus. Castor and Pollux were the Dioscuri, the "twins" of Gemini, the twin sons of Zeus (Jupiter) and Leda.

places.name: Museo Nazionale Romano
places.summary: The Museo Nazionale Romano is a museum with several branches in separate buildings throughout the city of Rome, Italy. It shows exhibits from the pre- and early history of Rome, with a focus on archaeological findings from the period of Ancient Rome.

places.name: Palazzo Barberini
places.summary: The Palazzo Barberini is a 17th-century palace in Rome, facing the Piazza Barberini in Rione Trevi. Today, it houses the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica, the main national collection of older paintings in Rome.

places.name: Tabularium
places.summary: The Tabularium was the official records office of ancient Rome and housed the offices of many city officials. Situated within the Roman Forum, it was on the front slope of the Capitoline Hill, below the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, to the southeast of the Arx.

places.name: Theatre of Pompey
places.summary: The Theatre of Pompey, also known by other names, was a structure in Ancient Rome built during the latter part of the Roman Republican era by Pompey the Great. Completed in 55 BC, it was the first permanent theatre to be built in Rome. Its ruins are located at Largo di Torre Argentina.

places.name: Chigi Palace
places.summary: The Chigi Palace is a palace and former noble residence in Rome which is the seat of the Council of Ministers and the official residence of the prime minister of Italy. It is located in the Piazza Colonna, next to Palazzo Montecitorio, seat of the Chamber of Deputies.

places.name: Equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius
places.summary: The equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius is an ancient Roman equestrian statue on the Capitoline Hill, Rome, Italy. It is made of bronze and stands 4.24 m tall. Although the emperor is mounted, the sculpture otherwise exhibits many similarities to the standing statues of Augustus.

sources.title: Equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius — Wikipedia

places.history: The original is on display in the Capitoline Museums, while the sculpture now standing in the open air at the Piazza del Campidoglio is a replica made in 1981 when the original was taken down for

places.name: Forum of Augustus
places.summary: The Forum of Augustus is one of the Imperial fora of Rome, Italy, built by Augustus. It includes the Temple of Mars Ultor. The incomplete forum and its temple were inaugurated in 2 BC, 40 years after they were first vowed.

places.name: Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri
places.summary: The Basilica of St. Mary of the Angels and of the Martyrs is a Catholic titular minor basilica and former Carthusian conventual church in Rome constructed in the ruined frigidarium and tepidarium of the Roman Baths of Diocletian in the Piazza della Repubblica.

sources.title: Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri — Wikipedia

places.name: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus
places.summary: The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, also known as the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, was the most important temple in Ancient Rome, located on the Capitoline Hill. It was surrounded by the Area Capitolina, a precinct where numerous shrines, altars, statues and victory trophies were displayed.

sources.title: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus — Wikipedia

places.name: Teatro dell'Opera di Roma
places.summary: The Teatro dell'Opera di Roma is an opera house in Rome, Italy. Originally opened in November 1880 as the 2,212 seat Costanzi Theatre, it has undergone several changes of name as well modifications and improvements. The present house seats 1,560.

places.name: Baths of Diocletian
places.summary: The Baths of Diocletian were public baths in ancient Rome. Named after emperor Diocletian and built from AD 298 to 306, they were the largest of the imperial baths.
places.history: The project was originally commissioned by Maximian upon his return to Rome in the autumn of 298 and was continued after his and Diocletian's abdication under Constantius, father of Constantine.The site houses the Basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri, built within the ruins in the 16th century, the Church of San Bernardo alle Terme, and part of the National Roman

places.name: Gardens of Vatican City
places.summary: The Gardens of Vatican City, also informally known as the Vatican Gardens in Vatican City, are private urban gardens and parks which cover more than half of the country, located in the west of the territory and owned by the Pope. There are some buildings, such as Vatican Radio and the Governor's Palace, within the gardens.

places.name: Temple of Caesar
places.summary: The Temple of Caesar or Temple of Divus Iulius, also known as Temple of the Deified Julius Caesar, delubrum, heroon or Temple of the Comet Star, was an ancient structure in the Roman Forum of Rome, Italy, located near the Regia and the Temple of Vesta.

places.name: Forum of Caesar
places.summary: The Forum of Caesar, also known by the Latin Forum Iulium or Forum Julium, Forum Caesaris, was a forum built by Julius Caesar near the Forum Romanum in Rome in 46 BC.

places.name: Fontana del Tritone
places.summary: Fontana del Tritone is a seventeenth-century fountain in Rome, by the Baroque sculptor Gian Lorenzo Bernini. Commissioned by his patron, Pope Urban VIII, the fountain is located in the Piazza Barberini, near the entrance to the Palazzo Barberini that Bernini helped to design and construct for the Barberini, Urban's family.
places.history: This fountain should be distinguished from the nearby Fontana dei Tritoni by Carlo Francesco Bizzaccheri in Piazza Bocca della Verità which features two

places.name: Sant'Ignazio
places.summary: The Church of St. Ignatius of Loyola at Campus Martius  is a Latin Catholic titular church, of deaconry rank, dedicated to Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Society of Jesus, located in Rome, Italy.
places.history: Built in Baroque style between 1626 and 1650, the church functioned originally as the chapel of the adjacent Roman College, which moved in 1584 to a new larger building and was renamed the Pontifical Gregorian University. It is one of the great 17th century preaching churches built by Counter-Reformation orders in the Centro

places.name: Santa Cecilia in Trastevere
places.summary: Santa Cecilia in Trastevere is a titular church and minor basilica located in Trastevere, Rome. Dedicated to Saint Cecilia, the patron saint of music, it has served as a cardinal titular church since the 5th century.
places.history: The present basilica, rebuilt under Pope Paschal I in the 9th century, is notable for its apse mosaic, frescoes by Pietro Cavallini, Baroque sculpture, and the revered relics of Saint Cecilia preserved beneath the high altar. Today, it remains the conventual church for the adjacent Benedictine abbey, and the feast of Saint Cecilia on 22 November continues to draw pilgrims, choirs, and musicians from around the

places.name: Pons Aemilius
places.summary: The Pons Aemilius is the oldest Roman stone bridge in Rome. Preceded by a wooden version, it was rebuilt in stone in the 2nd century BC. It once spanned the Tiber, connecting the Forum Boarium, the Roman cattle market, on the east with Trastevere on the west.
places.history: A single arch in mid-river is all that remains today, lending the bridge its name Ponte

places.name: Basilica Aemilia
places.summary: The Basilica Aemilia, or the Basilica Paulli, was a civil basilica in the Roman Forum. Lucius Aemilius Paullus initiated its construction, but the building was completed by his son, Paullus Aemilius Lepidus, in 34 BCE.
places.history: Under Augustus, it was reconstructed in 22 CE and was described by Pliny as one of the most beautiful examples of Roman architecture. Today, only fragments of the floorplan and colonnade remain, but a sculptural frieze from the basilica's interior was partially reconstructed and is now on display in the cloister of Santa Francesca

places.name: Forum Boarium
places.summary: The Forum Boarium was the cattle market or forum venalium of ancient Rome. It was located on a level piece of land near the Tiber between the Capitoline, the Palatine and Aventine hills.
places.history: As the site of the original docks of Rome and adjacent to the Pons Aemilius, the earliest stone bridge across the Tiber, the Forum Boarium experienced intense commercial

places.name: Basilica Julia
places.summary: The Basilica Julia was a civil basilica in the Roman Forum. Construction began under Julius Caesar in 46 BC and was completed by Augustus, who ultimately dedicated the basilica to Gaius and Lucius Caesar in 12 AD. It served as the headquarters for the centumviri, a judicial court that primarily dealt with matters of inheritance.
places.history: The basilica was destroyed by fire in 283 AD but was rebuilt and embellished throughout the late Imperial era. The three-story marble structure remained a prominent landmark in the Forum through much of Late Antiquity. By the Middle Ages, however, it had been stripped of its materials, and part of the structure was converted into a Christian church. places.name: Temple of Concord
places.summary: The Temple of Concord, or Temple of Concordia, in Rome refers to a series of temples dedicated to the Roman goddess Concordia, and erected at the western end of the Roman Forum.
places.history: The Romans believed that the earliest temple was built by Marcus Furius Camillus in 367 BC, but archeological evidence indicates the first shrine to Concordia on the site was constructed in 218 BC by Lucius Manlius Vulso. The temple was rebuilt in 121 BC by Lucius Opimius, following the killing of the Gaius Gracchus and his supporters, and again by the future emperor Tiberius between 7 BC and AD

places.name: Temple of Peace
places.summary: The Temple of Peace, also known as the Forum of Vespasian, was built in Rome in 71 AD under Emperor Vespasian in honour to Pax, the Roman goddess of peace.

places.name: Apollo and Daphne (Bernini)
places.summary: Apollo and Daphne is a life-sized marble sculpture by the Italian artist Gian Lorenzo Bernini, which was executed between 1622 and ‘25. It is regarded as one of the artistic marvels of the Baroque age.
places.history: The statue is housed in the Galleria Borghese in Rome, along with several other examples of the artist's most important early works. places.name: Teatro Argentina
places.summary: The Teatro Argentina is an opera house and theatre located in Largo di Torre Argentina, a square in Rome, Italy. One of the oldest theatres in Rome, it was constructed in 1731 and inaugurated on 31 January 1732 with Berenice by Domenico Sarro. It is built over part of the curia section of the Theatre of Pompey.
places.history: This curia was the location of the assassination of Julius

places.name: Baths of Trajan
places.summary: The Baths of Trajan were a massive thermae, a bathing and leisure complex, built in ancient Rome and dedicated under Trajan during the kalendae of July 109, shortly after the Aqua Traiana was dedicated.

places.name: Baths of Agrippa
places.summary: The Baths of Agrippa was a structure of ancient Rome, Italy, built by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa. It was the first of the great thermae constructed in the city, and also the first public bath.

places.name: Porta Pia
places.summary: Porta Pia was one of the northern gates in the Aurelian Walls of Rome, Italy. One of Pope Pius IV's civic improvements to the city, it is named after him.
places.history: Situated at the end of a new street, the Via Pia, it was designed by Michelangelo to replace the Porta Nomentana situated several hundred meters southwards, which was closed up at the same time. Construction began in 1561 and ended in 1565, after the artist's death. A 1561 bronze commemorative medal by Gian Federico Bonzagna shows an early plan by Michelangelo, very different from his final design. The façade on the outside of the city was completed in 1869 under the Neo-Classicist design by Virginio

places.name: Santi Cosma e Damiano
places.summary: The basilica of Santi Cosma e Damiano is a titular church in Rome, Italy. It is the conventual church of the General Curia of the Franciscan Third Order Regular.
places.history: The lower portion of the building is accessible through the Roman Forum and incorporates original Roman buildings, but the entrance to the upper level is outside the Forum facing the Via dei Fori

places.name: Santa Prassede
places.summary: The Basilica of Saint Praxedes, commonly known in Italian as Santa Prassede, is an early medieval titular church and minor basilica located near the papal basilica of Saint Mary Major, on Via di Santa Prassede, rione Monti in Rome, Italy. The current Cardinal Priest of Titulus Sancta Praxedis is Paul Poupard.

places.name: Forum of Nerva
places.summary: Forum of Nerva is an ancient structure in Rome, Italy, chronologically the next to the last of the Imperial fora built.

places.name: Galleria Doria Pamphilj
places.summary: The Galleria Doria Pamphilj is a large private art collection housed in the Palazzo Doria Pamphilj in Rome, Italy, between Via del Corso and Via della Gatta. The principal entrance is on the Via del Corso. The palace façade on Via del Corso is adjacent to a church, Santa Maria in Via Lata.
places.history: Like the palace, it is still privately owned by the princely Roman family Doria Pamphili. Tours of the state rooms often culminate in concerts of Baroque and Renaissance music, paying tribute to the setting and the masterpieces it

places.name: Palazzo Montecitorio
places.summary: Palazzo Montecitorio is a palace in Rome and the seat of the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of the Italian Parliament.

places.name: San Marco Evangelista al Campidoglio
places.summary: San Marco is a titular basilica in Rome dedicated to Saint Mark the Evangelist, located in the small Piazza di San Marco adjoining Piazza Venezia. It was first consecrated in 336 by Pope Mark and rebuilt in its present form in 833 by Pope Gregory IV. Today, the basilica is the national church of Venice in Rome.

sources.title: San Marco Evangelista al Campidoglio — Wikipedia

places.name: San Giovanni dei Fiorentini
places.summary: The Basilica of San Giovanni dei Fiorentini is a minor basilica and a titular church in the Ponte rione of Rome, Italy.

places.name: San Bernardo alle Terme
places.summary: San Bernardo alle Terme is a Baroque style, Catholic abbatial church located on Via Torino 94 in the rione Castro Pretorio of Rome, Italy. It is administered by the Cistercians.

places.name: Temple of Vespasian and Titus
places.summary: The so-called Temple of Vespasian and Titus is located in Rome at the western end of the Roman Forum between the Temple of Concordia and the Temple of Saturn. It was dedicated to the deified Vespasian. It was begun by Titus in 79 after Vespasian's death and Titus's succession.

places.name: Santo Stefano al Monte Celio
places.summary: The Basilica of St. Stephen in the Round on the Caelian Hill is an ancient basilica and titular church in Rome, Italy. Commonly named Santo Stefano Rotondo, the church is Hungary's "national church" in Rome, dedicated to both Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr, and Stephen I, the canonized first king of Hungary.

places.summary: Sant'Ambrogio e Carlo al Corso is a basilica church in Rome, Italy, facing onto the central part of the Via del Corso. The apse of the church faces across the street, the Mausoleum of Augustus on Via di Ripetta.

places.name: Pons Cestius
places.summary: The Pons Cestius is an ancient Roman bridge connecting the right bank of the Tiber with the west bank of Tiber Island in Rome, Italy. In Late Antiquity, the bridge was replaced and renamed the Pons Gratiani. It is also known as Ponte San Bartolomeo.

places.summary: The Pons Sublicius is the earliest known bridge of ancient Rome, spanning the Tiber River near the Forum Boarium downstream from the Tiber Island, near the foot of the Aventine Hill.
places.history: According to tradition, its construction was ordered by Ancus Marcius around 642 BC, but this date is approximate because there is no ancient record of its construction. Marcius wished to connect the newly fortified Janiculum Hill on the Etruscan side to the rest of Rome, augmenting the ferry that was there. places.summary: The Colossus of Nero was a 30-metre (98 ft) bronze statue that the Emperor Nero created in the vestibule of his Domus Aurea, the imperial villa complex which spanned a large area from the north side of the Palatine Hill, across the Velian ridge to the Esquiline Hill in Rome.

places.name: Fontana dell'Acqua Felice
places.summary: The Fontana dell'Acqua Felice, also called the Fountain of Moses, is a monumental fountain located in the Quirinale District of Rome, Italy. It marked the terminus of the Acqua Felice aqueduct restored by Pope Sixtus V. It was designed by Domenico Fontana and built in 1585–1588.

places.name: Santa Francesca Romana
places.summary: Santa Francesca Romana, previously known as Santa Maria Nova, is a Catholic church situated next to the Roman Forum in the rione Campitelli in Rome, Italy.

places.name: Santa Maria in Via Lata
places.summary: Santa Maria in Via Lata is a church on the Via del Corso, in Rome, Italy. It stands diagonal from the church of San Marcello al Corso. It is the stational church for Tuesday in the fifth week of lent.

places.summary: The Basilica of St. Bartholomew on the Island is a titular minor basilica, located in Rome, Italy. It was founded in 998 by Otto III, Holy Roman Emperor and contains the putative relics of St. Bartholomew the Apostle.

places.name: Santa Pudenziana
places.summary: The Basilica of Santa Pudentiana is the eldest Roman Catholic basilica built in the fourth century in Rome. The original shrine building dates back from the second century and is dedicated to Saint Pudentiana, sister to Praxedes the martyress. Both were daughters of Saint Pudens.

places.name: Santi Quattro Coronati
places.summary: Santi Quattro Coronati is an ancient titular and conventual minor basilica and Augustinian convent in Rome, Italy. The church dates back to the fourth or fifth century, and is devoted to four anonymous saints and martyrs.

places.name: Pontifical Ecclesiastical Academy
places.summary: The Pontifical Ecclesiastical Academy is one of the Roman Colleges of the Catholic Church. The academy is dedicated to training priests to serve in the diplomatic corps and the Secretariat of State of the Holy See.

places.name: Gardens of Sallust
places.summary: The Gardens of Sallust was an ancient Roman estate including a landscaped pleasure garden developed by the historian Sallust in the 1st century BC. It occupied a large area in the northeastern sector of Rome, in what would become Region VI, between the Pincian Hill and Quirinal Hill, near the Via Salaria and later Porta Salaria.

places.name: Basilica Ulpia
places.summary: The Basilica Ulpia was an ancient Roman civic building located in the Forum of Trajan. The Basilica Ulpia separates the temple from the main courtyard in the Forum of Trajan with the Trajan's Column to the northwest. It was named after Roman emperor Trajan whose full name was Marcus Ulpius Traianus.

places.name: Santi Giovanni e Paolo al Celio
places.summary: The Basilica of Saints John and Paul on the Caelian Hill is an ancient basilica church in Rome, located on the Caelian Hill. It was originally built in 398.

places.name: San Crisogono
places.summary: Basilica di San Crisogono is a titular church and minor basilica located in Trastevere, Rome. Established in the 4th century under Pope Sylvester I, it is one of the oldest parish churches in the city and has served as a cardinal titular church since early Christianity.
places.history: The present basilica, reconstructed under Cardinal Scipione Borghese in the early 17th century, is notable for its Baroque interior, and the extensive remains of the early Christian church preserved beneath the crypt. places.name: Palazzo della Cancelleria
places.summary: The Palazzo della Cancelleria is a Renaissance palace in Rome, Italy, situated between the present Corso Vittorio Emanuele II and the Campo de' Fiori, in the rione of Parione.

places.name: Sant'Andrea delle Fratte
places.summary: Sant'Andrea delle Fratte is a 17th-century basilica church in Rome, Italy, dedicated to St. Andrew. The Cardinal Priest of the Titulus S. Andreae Apostoli de Hortis is Ennio Antonelli.

places.name: Great Synagogue of Rome
places.summary: The Great Synagogue of Rome is an Orthodox Jewish congregation and synagogue, that is located at Lungotevere de' Cenci, in Rome, in Lazio, Italy. Designed by Vincenzo Costa and Osvaldo Armanni in an eclectic mix of Historicism and Art Nouveau styles, the synagogue was completed in 1904. It is the largest synagogue in Rome.

places.name: Porta Esquilina
places.summary: The Porta Esquilina was a gate in the Servian Wall, of which the Arch of Gallienus is extant today. Tradition dates it back to the 6th century BC, when the Servian Wall was said to have been built by the Roman king Servius Tullius. However modern scholarship and evidence from archaeology indicate a date in the fourth century BC.

places.name: Leonine City
places.summary: The Leonine City is the part of the city of Rome which, during the Middle Ages, was enclosed with the Leonine Wall, built by order of Pope Leo IV in the 9th century.

places.name: Via della Conciliazione
places.summary: Via della Conciliazione is a street in the Rione of Borgo within Rome, Italy. Roughly 500 metres (1,600 ft) in length, it connects Saint Peter's Square to the Castel Sant'Angelo on the western bank of the Tiber River. The road was constructed between 1936 and 1950, and it is the primary access route to the Square.

places.name: San Lorenzo in Damaso
places.summary: The Minor Basilica of St. Lawrence in Damaso or simply San Lorenzo in Damaso is a parish and titular church in central Rome, Italy that is dedicated to St. Lawrence, deacon and martyr. It is incorporated into the Palazzo della Cancelleria, which enjoys the extraterritoriality of the Holy See.

places.name: Temple of Venus Genetrix
places.summary: The Temple of Venus Genetrix is a ruined temple in the Forum of Caesar, Rome, dedicated to the Roman goddess Venus Genetrix, the founding goddess of the Julian gens. It was dedicated to the goddess on 26 September 46 BCE by Julius Caesar.

places.name: San Giovanni a Porta Latina
places.summary: San Giovanni a Porta Latina is a basilica church in Rome, Italy, near the Porta Latina of the Aurelian Wall.

places.name: San Vitale
places.summary: The early Christian imperial basilica of the Saints Martyrs Vitale, Valeria, Gervasio and Protasio known more commonly as the basilica of San Vitale and Compagni Martiri in Fovea or more simply as San Vitale al Quirinale. It is the oldest Catholic place of worship in the historic center of Rome, located in via Nazionale.
places.history: The imperial basilica of San Vitale al Quirinale, built under the pontificate of Pope Siricius after 386 and consecrated and richly decorated by Pope Innocent in 402 is the first public Christian basilica with a baptistery not founded on pre-existing pagan temples, mentioned in the Liber pontificalis, built by the Emperor Theodosius at the behest of Saint Ambrose of Milan, in honor of the miraculous discovery of the bodies of martyrs Gervasius and Protasius in Milan. places.name: San Silvestro in Capite
places.summary: The Basilica of Saint Sylvester the First, also known as, is a Roman Catholic minor basilica and titular church in Rome dedicated to Pope Sylvester I. It is located on the Piazza San Silvestro, at the corner of Via del Gambero and the Via della Mercede, and stands adjacent to the central Post Office.

places.name: Palazzo Colonna
places.summary: The Palazzo Colonna is a palatial block of buildings in central Rome, Italy, at the base of the Quirinal Hill, and adjacent to the church of Santi Apostoli. It is built in part over the ruins of an old Roman serapeum, and it has belonged to the prominent Colonna family for over twenty generations.

places.name: Aqua Alsietina
places.summary: The Aqua Alsietina is an ancient Roman aqueduct, erected sometime around 2 BC during the reign of emperor Augustus, and described in the De aquaeductu of the Roman official Frontinus. Because the aqueduct was constructed under Augustan rule, it was also called Aqua Auqusta.

places.name: Column of Antoninus Pius
places.summary: The Column of Antoninus Pius is a Roman honorific column in Rome, Italy, devoted in AD 161 to the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, in the Campus Martius, on the edge of the hill now known as Monte Citorio, and set up by his successors, the co-emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.

places.name: Palazzo Corsini
places.summary: The Palazzo Corsini is a late-baroque palace in Rome, erected for the Corsini family between 1730 and 1740 as an elaboration of the prior building on the site, a 15th-century villa of the Riario family, based on designs of Ferdinando Fuga. It is located in the Trastevere section of the city, and stands beside the Villa Farnesina.

places.name: Porta Capena
places.summary: The Porta Capena was a gate in the Servian Wall in Rome, Italy. The gate was located in the area of Piazza di Porta Capena, where the Caelian, Palatine and Aventine hills meet.

places.name: Porta San Paolo
places.summary: The Porta San Paolo is one of the southern gates in the 3rd-century Aurelian Walls of Rome, Italy. The Via Ostiense Museum is housed within the gatehouse. It is in the Ostiense quarter; just to the west is the Roman Pyramid of Cestius, an Egyptian-style pyramid, and beyond that is the Protestant Cemetery.

places.name: Santa Maria Antiqua
places.summary: Santa Maria Antiqua is a Catholic Marian church in Rome, Italy, built in the 5th century in the Forum Romanum, and for a long time the monumental access to the Palatine imperial palaces.

places.name: Septizodium
places.summary: The Septizodium was a building in ancient Rome. It was built in 203 AD by Emperor Septimius Severus.

places.name: San Marcello al Corso
places.summary: San Marcello al Corso is an ancient titular and conventual church in Rome, Italy. It has been served by friars of the Servite Order since c. 1375 and is the headquarters of their General Curia. The cardinal-protector of the church is normally of the order of cardinal priests, currently Giuseppe Betori.

places.name: Sant'Eustachio
places.summary: Sant'Eustachio is a Roman Catholic titular church and minor basilica in Rome, named for the martyr Saint Eustace. It is located on Via di Sant'Eustachio in the rione Sant'Eustachio, a block west of the Pantheon and via della Rotonda, and a block east of Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza and the Via della Dogana Vecchia.

places.name: Santi Bonifacio ed Alessio
places.summary: The Basilica dei Santi Bonifacio e(d) Alessio is a basilica, rectory church served by the Somaschans, and titular church for a cardinal-priest on the Aventine Hill in the third prefecture of central Rome, Italy.

places.name: Palazzo Borghese

places.name: San Giorgio in Velabro
places.summary: San Giorgio in Velabro is a Catholic church dedicated to St. George on Via del Velabro in the historic center of Rome in the Velabrum and the Ripa district.
places.history: The church—the result of the 9th century expansion of a previous diaconal building and subsequent remodeling—stands near the Arch of Janus in the small square of the Cloaca Maxima. places.name: San Lorenzo in Lucina
places.summary: The Minor Basilica of St. Lawrence in Lucina is a Roman Catholic parish, titular church, and minor basilica in central Rome, Italy. The basilica is located in Piazza di San Lorenzo in Lucina in the Rione Colonna, about two blocks behind the Palazzo Montecitorio, proximate to the Via del Corso.

places.name: Santa Susanna
places.summary: The Church of Saint Susanna at the Baths of Diocletian is a Catholic parish and Cistercian conventual church located on the Quirinal Hill in Rome, Italy. There has been a titular church associated to its site as far back as AD 280.

places.name: Santa Maria in Vallicella
places.summary: Santa Maria in Vallicella, also called Chiesa Nuova, is a church in Rome, Italy, which today faces onto the main thoroughfare of the Corso Vittorio Emanuele and the corner of Via della Chiesa Nuova.

places.summary: Nostra Signora del Sacro Cuore is a Catholic church dedicated to the Virgin Mary located in Rome's Piazza Navona.

places.summary: San Nicola in Carcere is an ancient titular church and minor basilica in Rome near the Forum Boarium in rione Ripa. It is constructed in the remains of the three temples of the Forum Holitorium and is one of the traditional stational churches of Lent.

places.name: Torre dei Conti
places.summary: The Torre dei Conti is a medieval fortified tower in Rome, Italy, located near the Colosseum and the Roman Forum.

places.name: Saepta Julia
places.summary: The Saepta Julia was a building in the Campus Martius of Rome, where citizens gathered to cast votes. The building was conceived by Julius Caesar and dedicated by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa in 26 BC. The building replaced an older structure, called the Ovile, built as a place for the comitia tributa to gather to cast votes.

places.name: Circus of Nero
places.summary: The Circus of Nero or Circus of Caligula was a circus in ancient Rome, located mostly in the present-day Vatican City.

places.name: Circus Flaminius
places.summary: The Circus Flaminius was a large, circular area in ancient Rome, located in the southern end of the Campus Martius near the Tiber River. It contained a small race-track used for obscure games, and various other buildings and monuments. It was "built", or sectioned off, by Gaius Flaminius in 221 BC.

places.name: Protestant Cemetery
places.summary: The Non-Catholic Cemetery, also referred to as the Protestant Cemetery or the English Cemetery, is a private cemetery in the rione of Testaccio in Rome.

It has Mediterranean cypress, pomegranate and other trees, and a grassy meadow. It is the final resting place of non-Catholics living in Rome or Italy in general, including but not exclusive to Protestants or British people.
